For nearly the whole history of our species, night was not merely the absence of day. It was a country in its own right, with its own laws, its own economy, its own dangers and graces, and going to bed was an act of border crossing. When the sun went down and the fire burned low, the world reorganized itself entirely. A neighbor ten steps from your door became invisible. Sound carried farther; every creak of the house became information; anything that moved out there was a shape, an intention, possibly a ghost. The darkness beyond the hearth was not the dimness of a modern city at midnight but something near-total, a darkness with texture and weight, in which any light was an event and any voice a message from another world.

We assume our ancestors slept through that country in one long dive from dusk to dawn, the way we do. It seems they mostly didn't. In the 1990s the historian Roger Ekirch began collecting references to sleep in diaries, letters, court depositions, medical texts, and literature, and he found the same strange pattern everywhere: Europeans before the industrial era, and people in many other pre-industrial societies, slept in two segments. There was a "first sleep" that began an hour or two after dusk, and a "second sleep" that ran to dawn, and between them, around midnight, a calm waking hour or two. People knew this interval so well they had names for it. They called it "the watch," or simply "watching." They got up. They tended the fire, prayed, read if they could afford candles, talked quietly with a spouse, went out to see a neighbor or, court records show, a lover. They lay still and thought, which may be the most enviable item on the list. The phrase "first sleep" turns up in Homer, in Chaucer, in French and Italian sources and colonial American diaries; the Tiv of Nigeria used the same division. Monks rising for vigils in the middle of the night may simply have been marking a seam the species already had. Ekirch's argument, now widely accepted, is that segmented sleep was the human default for millennia, and that artificial evening light fused the two halves into one. When we wake at three in the morning and feel broken about it, we may be feeling an heirloom knocking.

(~270 words.)

The old night had legal code as well as biology. Our word curfew preserves its first commandment: couvre-feu, cover the fire, the bell rung in medieval towns to douse the hearths. City gates shut at dusk; travelers who missed the hour waited outside the walls for dawn, among whatever else was out there. To be abroad after dark without good reason was itself an offense — "nightwalking" — and watchmen patrolled with lanterns, calling out the hour and the weather, like human foghorns. The rich moved at night behind link-boys carrying flaming torches for hire. The poor moved by moonlight, which was genuine infrastructure: the harvest moon was worth real labor, letting farmers bring in the grain by its light. And fear had its own vocabulary. Night was when the day's surveillance was off. A servant's room, a shared bed, a hedge between two houses — all became private countries after the fire went down. For the rich, night was expensive and therefore dim, all those candles; for the poor it was the one part of the day paid to no one.
